10429-miss-lulu-bett:
Zona Gale published this novel in 1921, following its heroine month by month from April through September. Lulu Bett lives with the Deacon family, serving at table under a gas jet, while Mr. Deacon jokes nightly and Mrs. Deacon speaks gently to all. The small tulip plant on the table hints at Lulu's own stifled life.

As months pass, Lulu faces family duty, a child's needs, and a chance for a life of her own. Gale writes with humor, pity, and close detail about women's work in a small town. Readers get a keen, humane novel of a woman finding voice, later famous on stage and in film.
10440-tutt-and-mr-tutt:
Arthur Train published this law story collection in 1919, following the firm of Tutt and Tutt, attorneys in New York. The elder Mr. Tutt and his junior partner Tutt take cases where chance, not grand design, often decides the outcome. Train, himself a lawyer, writes with wit and inside knowledge.

The human element, mock hen and mock turtle, Samuel and Delilah, the dog Andrew, and Lallapaloosa Limited fill the set. A murder client who boasts he would kill again opens the first tale. Readers get a clever, humane book of legal comedy and courtroom craft.
12556-a-master-of-fortune-being-further-:
Cutcliffe Hyne's 1898 sequel, A Master of Fortune, continues the adventures of Captain Kettle, illustrated by Stanley L. Wood. A frontispiece shows Kettle in high rubber thigh boots and black oilskins. Chapters promise quarantine, a little wooden god with eyes, a quick way with rebels, a new republic, the looting of the Indian Sheriff, wire-milkers, a derelict and a captured heiress.

Kettle, a seafaring adventurer of the old school, meets rebels, republics and rogues with cunning and nerve. Hyne writes brisk adventure fiction for readers who liked the sea, the tropics and a hero who masters fortune by wit. The book is a lively late Victorian boys' and men's tale, episodic, colourful and unashamedly imperial in flavour.
13408-our-stage-and-its-critics-by-e-f-s:
E. F. S. of the Westminster Gazette writes from inside Edwardian theatre criticism in 1910. He describes what a dramatic critic needs, how he works under deadline, what stock phrases he leans on, and how fear of libel shapes his copy. Youthful sympathy, jaded routine, unpaid labour, and a heavy letter bag all get their chapters.

Later sections sort plays by type, from pseudo-historical and horrible dramas to immorality, Scripture, anecdotal, and supernatural plays, and judge managers who pander to vulgar taste. Performers pass in review, including a rustic Phèdre compared with Bernhardt. The book is both a defence of the critic's craft and a candid look at its limits.
16182-the-letters-of-robert-browning-and:
Volume one of the letters of Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett Barrett, in a fourth impression from Smith, Elder in 1900, covers their courtship years of 1845 and 1846. Portraits and facsimiles illustrate the two volumes. A note by their son explains the choice to publish. The letters were all that ever passed between his parents, since after marriage they were never separated. His father had kept them in an inlaid box into which they exactly fitted, letter beside letter.

The letters trace a famous love story from first admiration to secret engagement and flight, in two brilliant, candid voices. Readers meet Victorian poetry's great romance at its most intimate. The collection remains a landmark of literary love letters.
17444-general-scott:
General Marcus J. Wright wrote this life of Winfield Scott for the Great Commanders series, edited by James Grant Wilson and published in New York in 1894, with copyright dated 1893. Scott, the long-serving American general, stands in a series beside Farragut, Taylor, Jackson, Greene, Johnston, and Thomas. Wright, himself a general, writes as a soldier judging a soldier.

The book follows Scott's campaigns and commands across a career that stretched from the War of 1812 to the opening of the Civil War. Readers get a compact, late nineteenth-century military biography, more interested in command decisions and service than in private life. It remains a handy starting point for Scott's place among America's early generals.
18124-sir-walter-scott:
Richard H. Hutton wrote Sir Walter Scott, printed in London in 1878 by Macmillan. Hutton draws most of his little book from Lockhart's Life of Scott in ten volumes. That life is the great source for Scott's character and story, checked against the Ballantyne brothers' own accounts where they differ.

Chapters run from ancestry, parentage, and childhood to youth, love, marriage, and the early poems and border minstrelsy. Hutton writes with a critic's warmth and a biographer's brevity. The book is a fine, short introduction to Scott, best read before the Waverley novels themselves.
18129-south-with-scott:
Rear Admiral Edward Evans wrote this first-hand account of Captain Robert Falcon Scott's Terra Nova expedition to Antarctica. Evans served on the voyage, and his book names the shore parties, sailors, stewards, cooks, and dog drivers who made up the party. Maps and photographs from the trip appear with the text.

The chapters follow the whole course of the expedition. They cover the outfit and aims, the voyage south, and the winter in Antarctica. Depot trips and the climb over the Beardmore Glacier lead to the attainment of the Pole. The book ends with the search party that found Scott's party after its last march. The book reads as a plain record by a man who was there.
18589-the-act-of-incorporation-and-the-b:
Printed at Boston in 1864, this short pamphlet gives the legal frame of the Massachusetts Homoeopathic Medical Society. Its first part reprints the 1856 act that made Samuel Gregg, William Wesselhoeft, Luther Clark, and their associates a corporation, able to hold up to fifty thousand dollars in property. Members were excused from militia muster under the act.

The second part prints the bylaws revised and adopted on April 13, 1864. They set out officers, from president and vice presidents to secretaries, treasurer, librarian, and five censors, plus rules for electing members and testing candidates for skill and good character. The pamphlet is a plain record of a medical society's founding rules.
18840-a-dream-of-empire-or-the-house-of-:
William Henry Venable's historical novel, published by Dodd, Mead in 1901, takes its second title from the house of Blennerhassett. It opens on the first of May, when Peter Taylor, an English overseer, watches a slave trim a lawn while spring fever idles the household.

Later chapters bring a noted character to Pittsburgh, a conspiracy, diamond cut diamond, the voyage of the Buckeye, a midnight departure, and flight and surrender. An eccentric visitor, a doctor and his Lucrece, and a patriot not to be tampered with people the plot. The novel follows western ambition and intrigue in the early republic, closing with what became of its schemers and lovers.
18932-mental-defectives-and-sexual-offen:
A committee of inquiry appointed by Sir Maui Pomare, New Zealand's minister of health, issued this report in 1925, laid on the table of the House of Representatives. Its chairman was W. H. Triggs, joined by medical leaders including Sir Donald McGavin, Sir Frederic Truby King of child welfare, J. Sands Elliott of the British Medical Association's New Zealand branch, and Dr. Ada G. Paterson.

The report examines mental defect and sexual offending as the committee understood them in the 1920s, with recommendations for care, control, and law. Its language and categories belong to its era and now read as dated and, in places, harsh. Readers get a primary source for the history of medicine, law, and social policy in New Zealand, important for understanding past attitudes rather than as a guide to present practice.
20932-advice-to-a-young-man-upon-first-g:
Joy at a young man's entry to Oxford opens Advice to a Young Man in ten letters. The writer's own Oxford days warm his hopes for the youth's gain. Edward Berens frames his counsel as trust in the place's deep benefits.

Study, friends, money, faith, and time all get plain, fatherly treatment here. Such letter guides steered new undergraduates through a famed, risky world. Berens warns and cheers in equal measure across the ten letters. The book preserves the morals and manners expected at Oxford in the early 1800s, in a voice both kind and firmly of its age.
21634-the-life-and-adventures-of-nat-lov:
Nat Love tells his own life in The Life and Adventures of Nat Love, published at Los Angeles in 1907. In the cattle country he was better known as Deadwood Dick. The book is dedicated to his wife, Alice Love, and illustrated with family pictures.

Love begins with slavery days on the old plantation, and a stolen jug that gave him his first drunk. Freedom, his father's death, and work at a dollar and a half a month follow. Then come Texas cowboys, brand reading, round-ups, and fights on the trail. Few Black cowboys left so full a record of the range.
26131-james-watt:
Andrew Carnegie's 1905 life of James Watt begins with the inventor's birth at Greenock on January 19, 1736, and his youth in a family of schoolmasters and town officers. Chapters follow Watt from Glasgow to London and back. They cover his capture by the problem of steam and his first partnership with Roebuck. Then comes the famous partnership with Matthew Boulton at Soho near Birmingham.

Carnegie gives close attention to Watt's patents, his engines for mines and mills, and his later years as a respected man of science. The book also sketches Watt the man: careful, anxious, and inventive by habit. It remains a readable account of how one craftsman's engine helped drive the industrial age.
27106-kinematics-of-mechanisms-from-the-:
Eugene S. Ferguson's Kinematics of Mechanisms from the Time of Watt, Smithsonian paper 27, traces machine motion from James Watt onward. Watt, in an inventive tour de force, altered the steam engine with a separate condenser and created a whole new family of linkages, working largely by empirical feel.

Ferguson follows the problem of drawing a straight line through scholars, mechanicians, and mechanisms in America from 1875 to 1955. His argument holds that a highly developed intuitive sense, reinforced by knowledge of the past, remains indispensable to designing successful mechanisms. The paper is number 27 in the museum's series. Ferguson later taught mechanical engineering at Iowa State University. Watt's linkages let engines move in new ways.
290-the-stark-munro-letters-being-series:
J. Stark Munro, a young doctor, writes twelve letters to his friend Herbert Swanborough between 1881 and 1884. The Stark Munro Letters, edited and arranged by Arthur Conan Doyle, follow a beginner facing money trouble and religious doubt. Doyle's preface hands the letters on as a plain account.

Two letters, the fifth and ninth, carry excisions, but the rest stand as written. Munro's struggles with practice, faith, and friendship give the book its shape. Doyle promises strength to any young man in the same valley. The novel reads as a frank portrait of starting out.
29624-sir-walter-scott:
George Saintsbury wrote this life of Sir Walter Scott in the Famous Scots Series, beside lives of Carlyle, Ramsay, Burns, and Boswell by other hands. Its chapters run from life till marriage through early literary work, the verse romances, and later years. Saintsbury notes Scott's remote kinship with gentle families on both sides, tracing his great-grandfather to the Laird of Raeburn, grandson of Walter Scott of Harden.

The book follows Scott from border boy to novelist, poet, and laird, with the warmth of a fellow man of letters. Readers of Scottish literature will find a compact, classic life of the wizard of the North, written by a critic who loved his subject.
34106-little-women-letters-from-the-hous:
Jessie Bonstelle and Marian DeForest selected these letters from the house of Alcott, published in Boston in 1914 by Little, Brown. A frontispiece shows Orchard House, the Alcott homestead. Chapters run from the really, truly true and the Alcott boy and man through the Alcott children and baby book to letters with children, the mother's influence, and children's diaries.

Girlhood and womanhood, friendships and beliefs, and a chronology close the book, with pictures of Bronson Alcott, letters to Louisa and Elizabeth, and daguerreotypes of Abigail May and Anna Alcott. The volume offers a warm, intimate Alcott family album in letters.
36004-the-pullman-boycott:
Burns wrote The Pullman Boycott, a complete history of the great railroad strike of 1894. His own printing company at Saint Paul issued the book that same year, under a copyright in his name. The catalog title is that copyright line. The strike had shut the nation's railways that summer.

The chapters follow the fight in order. The American Railway Union comes first, then the boycott of Pullman cars. Eugene Debs, the union's president, appeals to the men. The federal government sides with the managers, troops move to Blue Island, and Governor Altgeld of Illinois protests. Fire and bloodshed follow, then the indictment of Debs, his jail term, and his trial. Blacklisting of the strikers closes the tale. The book is a near instant history of the strike that broke the first great industrial union in America.
36188-the-judicial-murder-of-mary-e-surr:
Judicial Murder of Mary Surratt, by David Miller DeWitt, attacks a famous trial. John Murphy of Baltimore issued the book in eighteen ninety five. DeWitt argues the judgment on Surratt was unjust and cannot stand. A long Carlyle style passage on unjust judgments fronts the work.

Contents open with a reign of terror and a bureau of military injustice. Part one, The Murder, treats the opening of the trial court first. Was she ironed, the first chapter asks of the prisoner treatment there. Bias of the judges and insults to counsel form the next chapter. Conduct of the trial itself is then weighed in close detail.
37820-chronicles-of-martin-hewitt:
Chronicles of Martin Hewitt is a collection of detective stories by Arthur Morrison, published in New York by D Appleton and Company in 1896. It appeared as number 191 of Appletons' Town and Country Library. Morrison was already known for Tales of Mean Streets. Martin Hewitt is his cool, methodical investigator.

Six cases fill the volume. The Ivy Cottage Mystery opens the set, told by Hewitt's journalist friend. The Nicobar Bullion Case and the Holford Will Case follow. The Case of the Missing Hand and the Case of Laker, Absconded, continue the run. The Case of the Lost Foreigner closes the book. Morrison wrote Hewitt as a deliberate contrast to flashier detectives of the day. His man solves by patience and common sense, in stories built like clean machines.
38415-gas-engines-and-producer-gas-plant:
Mathot, a Belgian engineer, wrote Gas-Engines and Producer-Gas Plants as a hands-on treatise, put out in New York by Munn in 1905. Kaempffert turned the French text into English. Dugald Clerk, a famed gas engineer, praised the book in a warm preface.

Mathot sets out how gas engines and gas plants work, and how to pick and set up an engine. He gives the marks of sound running and the care such plants need day by day. A last part treats oil engines and their fuels. Clerk notes that no book then went so deep into set-up and upkeep. Plant owners and engineers get tested rules from a man who had run and judged such engines for years.
39084-william-hickling-prescott:
Harry Thurston Peck's Prescott, in the English Men of Letters series from Macmillan in 1905, gives the life of the American historian William Hickling Prescott. Peck acknowledges his debt to George Ticknor's 1864 life and its letters. Ten chapters run from the New England historians and Prescott's early years through the choice of a career, success, mid career, and the last ten years. Three chapters then judge the books: Ferdinand and Isabella, the Conquest of Mexico, and the Conquest of Peru with Philip the Second.

The first chapter argues that the early republic was three separate nations in culture, and reads American literature by sections. Peck closes with Prescott's rank as an historian. The dedication is to William Archibald Dunning of Columbia, where Peck wrote in March 1905. The series format gives a short critical life, more essay than archive.
39527-the-early-life-and-adventures-of-s:
The Early Life and Adventures of Sylvia Scarlett is a novel by Compton Mackenzie. The author had fame from past tales of street sin and a country house. Rights date the work to the year nineteen eighteen. Its first scene is set in Paris in the year eighteen forty seven.

A gay young lord sips coffee at dawn fresh from a ball at a great house. Town talk has paired him with the girl of that house as his bride. Wed lock, he holds, is no call that presses on his mind that dawn. From that seed grows the life of Sylvia, his bold girl child. Stage life, flight, and free love mark her famed wild course.
39660-sylvia-michael-the-later-adventure:
Compton Mackenzie continues his heroine's story in book three of Sylvia Scarlett, issued by Harper and Brothers in 1919. His author's note owns the oddity: the volume is really part of the longer work, published separately for the difficulties of production.

No Passport Office stood in Bucharest in 1915, he warns, and no portraits in the book are real. By the time Sylvia reaches Paris, she blames nobody but herself. She had tried to snatch artistic success and domestic bliss at once. She never seriously chose between them, and now she has lost both. Her confidence to Olive and her trust in Arthur's devotion left nothing but flight. With the engagement broken, she feels no bitterness toward Arthur. The surprise is that he should have won through the wreck with credit.
39965-american-big-game-hunting-the-book:
Roosevelt and Grinnell ran a book of big game hunts for their club. The Boone and Crockett Club is named in its sub-title in full. The book's rights date to 1893, this form to 1901. Anderson's buffalo tale leads the set of hunt tales. Wister writes on the white goat and its wild home ground.

A day with the elk and old days in the Black Hills come next. Rogers takes big game in the Rockies in his long piece. Roosevelt's own piece chases the prongbuck at full pace. Grinnell tells of buffalo days, and Pickett of nights with grizzlies. Hague holds the Yellowstone a fine game keep. Wild west fans get a crown book.
41446-the-heart-of-pinocchio-new-adventu:
The Heart of Pinocchio, new adventures of the celebrated little puppet, was written by Collodi Nipote, the pen name of Paolo Lorenzini, and adapted from the Italian by Virginia Watson. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in 1919, with drawings by J R Flanagan. The first chapter tells how Pinocchio discovered that he had a heart and had become a real boy. The second shows him learning the advantages of his wooden body.

Lorenzini was the nephew of Carlo Collodi, the creator of Pinocchio, and he continued the puppet's story for a new generation. The book appeared in Harper's Twilight Series beside Alice in Wonderland and The Water Babies. Its Pinocchio faces fresh scrapes and fresh lessons, with the same rascal energy that made the original a classic of the nursery shelf.
44465-cynthia-with-an-introduction-by-ma:
Leonard Merrick wrote Cynthia, a novel issued at New York by Dutton in 1919 with an introduction by Maurice Hewlett. Two friends sit outside the Café des Tribunaux at Dieppe at the hour of coffee and liqueurs on an August evening. One of them, Humphrey Kent, is falling in love. The other, an untidy and gloomy little man named Turquand, wastes advice on him.

Turquand lays out Kent's luck: a clerk in the city a year ago, placing three short tales a year at a guinea each. An aunt's legacy of a thousand pounds freed him, and his first novel won reviews any novelist in England would envy. Marriage now, Turquand argues, would fly in the face of providence, since the income of a new writer is unknown.
47306-tobias-smollett:
Oliphant Smeaton wrote a life of Tobias Smollett for the Famous Scots set. Charles Scribner's Sons issued the set in New York. Twelve chapters run from birth and school to last days and death. Smeaton ends with views of Smollett as novelist, writer of the past, and poet.

Smeaton opens with praise from Sir Walter Scott for the poet's spark in all good fiction. He grants that fair judgment of Smollett is hard, since the man gave much cause for blame. Roderick Random, Peregrine Pickle, and Humphry Clinker mark the high points. Readers gain a brisk life of a rough, gifted Scots author.
47617-edinburgh-under-sir-walter-scott:
Edinburgh Under Sir Walter Scott, by Fyfe, with an introduction by Rait, was published by Constable in 1906. Its thesis opens the introduction. From about the death of Samuel Johnson in 1784 to that of Walter Scott in 1832, Edinburgh, rather than London, was the intellectual centre of the kingdom. Rait concedes the counter-examples at once: Sheridan, Bentham, Blake, Lamb, and Keats all belong to London in that period.

Even so, the Edinburgh society Scott knew in youth and prime held a long series of remarkable men. Robertson the historian, Hugh Blair, and John Home, author of Douglas, are named. So is Henry Mackenzie, the Man of Feeling. The Edinburgh Review's influence, and its rival the Quarterly, run through the story.
50093-keeping-up-with-william-in-which-t:
Irving Bacheller published Keeping Up with William in 1918, as a wartime sequel to his bestseller Keeping Up with Lizzie. Its subtitle promises the Honorable Socrates Potter talking of the relative merits of sense common and preferred. Gaar Williams drew the cartoons. Bacheller dedicates the book, and its proceeds, to the children of France and Belgium made fatherless by the war.

The narrator visits Potter, the famous country lawyer, at his Connecticut office in January 1918. The old man sits in the same chair as seven years before, feet on the table, a spaniel by the fire. Portraits of Lincoln, Webster, and Sumner hang over the mantel. The talk turns at once to the great fight between democracy and, Potter interrupts, deviltry.
51016-the-pipes-of-war-a-record-of-achie:
The Pipes of War records what pipers of Scottish and overseas regiments did in the war of 1914 to 1918. Brevet-Colonel Sir Bruce Seton and Pipe-Major John Grant made the book, with help from writers such as Neil Munro and Philip Gibbs. It was printed in Glasgow in 1920, close on the war's end.

A front picture shows Piper James Richardson, who won the Victoria Cross, playing at Regina Trench. The words that open the book say the pipes spoke of home wherever Scots fought, at the height of battle and by lonely graves alike. Regimental pipers often played men over the top and paid for it with their lives. This record names their deeds while the men who heard them still lived to tell the tale.
51030-secret-service-under-pitt:
Fitzpatrick, the Irish biographer, wrote Secret Service Under Pitt as a companion to his volumes on Daniel O'Connell. The hosted copy opens with pages of press praise for the O'Connell volumes, the private correspondence and memoirs issued by John Murray of London. The Standard, the Times, the Daily Telegraph, and the Athenaeum are quoted, and Gladstone himself, writing in The Nineteenth Century, calls O'Connell both a great man and a good man.

Only after those testimonials does the title page of Secret Service Under Pitt arrive, naming Fitzpatrick as author. The subject is the secret service run under Pitt: its money, its agents, and its informers. Fitzpatrick brought to it the same habits the reviewers praised in the O'Connell work: patience in gathering letters and care in arranging them. Students of Irish politics were his first readers.
51357-the-autobiography-of-phineas-pett:
Phineas Pett speaks for himself in The Autobiography of Phineas Pett, edited by W G Perrin and printed for the Navy Records Society in 1918 as volume fifty-one of its publications. Pett was the great shipwright of the early Stuart navy. The edition supplies missing words in brackets, as the preface notes.

Archaic and nautical terms are explained in the footnotes. The society's council list fronts the volume, with the king as patron and Lord George Hamilton as president. A shipwright's own life, kept in his own words, is a rare survival from the dockyards of his age. Perrin presents it plainly.
53285-historical-characters-mackintosh-t:
Sir Henry Lytton Bulwer drew short lives of five men who shaped their age. Macmillan issued the one-volume form in London in 1900, after first forms from 1867 onward. The five are Mackintosh, Talleyrand, Canning, Cobbett, and Peel. Bulwer gave the book to Lord Lytton in a warm signed note.

Bulwer says he meant to paint an age through the men who best stood for its types. War, reform, free speech, and rule all find a face here. He grants flaws in the work, born of travel and ill health. Readers gain brisk, fair sketches of famed minds from the French revolt onward.
53299-a-christmas-hamper-a-volume-of-pic:
A Christmas Hamper is a volume of pictures and stories for little folks, from Nelson and Sons of London, Edinburgh, and New York. It opens with a verse about a hamper full of sweet things for Christmas night. Its contents mix short tales and rhymes: A Very Naughty Little Person, The Little Tiny Thing, A Lesson in Manners, The Prize Boat, and The Little Thief in the Pantry.

The first poem gives a small child's excuses for slammed doors, knotted shoe-strings, and blotted copy-books. The tale of Poor Uncle Tom follows: Hugh, Lily, and little Tom meet a funny old gentleman in the wood who brings sweets from his pocket. Talk turns to the uncle Tom was named for, lost at sea, whose monument stands in the church. The talk leaves the children grave.
54980-the-country-of-sir-walter-scott:
The Country of Sir Walter Scott is a travel and literary book by Charles Olcott, issued in 1913. Olcott had written a like book on George Eliot and her novels. Photographs by the author himself illustrate the volume. He dedicates it to his wife, the companion of his travels, whose help gave him much of his material.

The contents move through Scott's works in order, one chapter to a book. It opens with the making of Sir Walter and his first long poem. Waverley, Guy Mannering, The Antiquary, and Old Mortality follow in turn. Rob Roy, Ivanhoe, and Kenilworth each get a chapter, as the tour ties places to tales. The method is simple: walk the ground Scott wrote from, and read the books against the land.
55896-with-mask-and-mitt:
Albertus Dudley wrote With Mask and Mitt, a school baseball story published by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in Boston in 1906. Charles Copeland drew the pictures. The book belongs to the Phillips Exeter series, alongside Following the Ball, Making the Nine, and In the Line. The title points to the catcher's gear, and the frontispiece shows a runner nailed at the base as the game is won.

The early chapters bring two apprentices into the school team and hail the pitcher. A chapter list full of schoolboy troubles follows: a marplot named Payner, a captain's troubles, a set-back for O'Connell, and the third string fighting for places. Dudley built the series on the diamond rivalries and loyalties of boarding school life. Making the nine matters as much as lessons there. Each season tests new boys trying to earn a place.
58075-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of Arnold Bennett, the English novelist. Like Widger's other Gutenberg indexes, the file is a finding aid. It lists Bennett's books as the project issued them, then prints the table of contents of each volume in turn. A reader can survey a whole career on one screen before choosing where to start.

The shelf is a large one. The Old Wives' Tale, Clayhanger, Hilda Lessways, and Anna of the Five Towns stand for the Five Towns novels. The Grand Babylon Hotel, The Card, and Denry the Audacious show his lighter side. Practical books appear too: How to Live on 24 Hours a Day, Literary Taste, and The Author's Craft among them. Bennett wrote fiction, plays, journals, and self-help with equal energy. Widger's index gathers the Gutenberg editions of that output into a single ordered list.
58158-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Louisa May Alcott, arranging links to every Alcott text the project then held. The contents open with Flower Fables, her first book, and Little Women, her immortal one. Little Men follows, in plain and illustrated form.

Eight Cousins, Rose in Bloom, Jack and Jill, and An Old-Fashioned Girl fill the middle of the list. Jo's Boys and Under the Lilacs continue the family shelf. Hospital Sketches recalls her Civil War nursing, and Aunt Jo's Scrap-Bag runs to four volumes. Such indexes were the project's finding aids in its growth years. Widger made many of them, author by author. The page is a door key to a beloved writer's whole free shelf.
58572-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Tobias Smollett is a finding aid compiled by David Widger. It gathers the tables of contents of Smollett's books as issued by that library. Six works stand at its head in a short master list. The body of the file then prints each book's contents in full.

The Expedition of Humphry Clinker leads the set of novels and travels. Its contents are a chain of letters between a fixed circle of writers. Bath and Gloucester addresses recur through the long list of letters. Peregrine Pickle and Roderick Random follow among the adventures. Sir Launcelot Greaves and Ferdinand Count Fathom complete the fiction shelf. Travels through France and Italy stand beside the novels in the index.
58797-david-crockett:
Charles Fletcher Allen wrote David Crockett: Scout, a life of the Tennessee frontiersman for young readers, copyrighted by the Lippincott company in 1911. The subtitle piles up Crockett's roles: small boy, pilgrim, mountaineer, soldier, bear hunter, congressman, and defender of the Alamo. Frank McKernan drew the front picture.

Chapters follow Davy from his boyhood and his start for Virginia into the woods as a scout. Readers get hard fighting, a cabin in the wilderness, earthquakes, bear hunts, and a great Mississippi flood. Then come Congress, fame, the rifle he called Betsy, and the road to Texas. The book ends at the Alamo. Allen writes a rousing hero tale that kept Crockett's legend before new generations.
60791-the-war-with-russia-its-origin-and:
The War with Russia: Its Origin and Cause is a pamphlet by John Alfred Langford, printed at London in 1855. It is a reply to the letter of J Bright, member of Parliament, who had spoken against the Crimean War. Langford opens amid the din of arms. The less harmful but perhaps not less potent war of opinion, he writes, is as busy as in the piping times of peace.

A vast majority of the nation, he says, believe in the justness of England's position. They believe she exhausted every means, and even went beyond the strict line of national respect, to stay the hand of Russia. They hold that no other course was open to her. She must stoutly oppose further encroachments on the rights and liberties of Turkey if she wished to preserve her own dearly-won liberties.
61245-sir-walter-scott:
Andrew Lang wrote this life of Sir Walter Scott for the Literary Lives series, edited by W Robertson Nicoll, and it came out in New York in 1906. Lang knew Scott's poems and novels well. He tells the story of the great Scots writer from birth to death in six chapters, with portraits and views of Abbotsford, Scott's home.

The chapters move from Scott's roots, childhood, and first love through his early married life and his work gathering old ballads. Lang then covers the long poems that made Scott famed, the founding of a review, and the run of Waverley novels that changed fiction. The last part deals with Scott's money ruin and his death. Readers get a clear, brief life of a writer whose tales of Scotland won fans round the world.
62668-the-life-of-hector-berlioz-as-writ:
Katharine F Boult translated and introduced The Life of Hector Berlioz as Written by Himself in His Letters and Memoirs, published in London in 1903. Berlioz tells his own story, from his birth at La Cote Saint-Andre in 1803. Chapter heads show a medical student in Paris who gives up anatomy for music, against his father's will.

Later heads mark poverty, failure, and a night at the opera that changes him. Henriette, the actress Harriet Smithson, enters; then a first concert, the Prix de Rome won with Sardanapalus, and marriage. The Requiem, newspaper bondage, and tours to Russia and London fill the middle. The Trojans and a last return to Estelle, his first love, close the arc. A chronology sets the works in order. Few composers have left so vivid an account of themselves.
62932-mother-s-knitter-containing-some-p:
A writer signing only with initials made this little knitting book, Mother's Knitter, printed at London by Hatchards in 1882. It holds patterns for things for little children, as its title page promises. The contents run to a baby's boot in three sizes, a child's jacket, a sock, a frock, a petticoat, a shawl in daisy stitch, and a tam o' shanter cap.

The general remarks open with plain rules: always cast off loosely unless told otherwise. She weighs the wools of the day, merino, Andalusian, and eider yarn among them, and warns that the size of wool and needles matters in trying a pattern. An index of things in knitting books closes the volume. It is a mother's working book, worn by use.
65757-last-essays-of-maurice-hewlett:
Last Essays is a posthumous set of essays by Maurice Hewlett, first issued at London in 1924. A note at the front is candid about its making. Lovers of Hewlett's work will understand, it says, that these essays lack the severe revision he would have given them. His executors chose in each doubtful case to print the essays as he left them.

Thanks are given to the papers and magazines where some of them first appeared, among them The Times and The Cornhill. The contents open with a return to the nest, then a piece that starts as a prayer. Death enters the early heads, in the plain way of a last book. Hewlett had been a well known novelist and essayist of his generation. These final pieces, unrevised, show his hand at its most direct.
66962-in-texas-with-davy-crockett:
John McIntyre, who also sent boys west with Daniel Boone and Kit Carson, published this Texas adventure with Penn Publishing of Philadelphia in nineteen fourteen. Two boys, Walter Jordan and Ned Chandler, are traveling down the Mississippi by steamboat when they spot a man, Sam Davidge, shadowing them, and the suspicion shapes the voyage.

The chapters promise bear hunting, a buffalo hunt, an attack by Comanches, and a fight with Mexicans before the climax at the battle of the Alamo. Davy Crockett himself enters in the fifth chapter, and the book closes with a short sketch of the life of David Crockett for readers wanting the facts behind the hero. Illustrations by John Huybers include the Alamo fight. McIntyre wrote history as boys' adventure, and this volume belongs to the shelf of frontier tales that taught young Americans their national legends.
70332-the-declaration-and-confession-of-:
The Declaration and Confession of Robert Watt is a last words tract, out at Edinburgh in seventeen ninety-four. Watt wrote, signed, and gave it the night past his death for high treason, set for the next day. Two church men, one the head of the town school, vouch that the print is word for word from his hand. A note past his goods goes with the tract.

In a note to the law man of the town Watt leaves his watch, clothes, and small goods to a man he owes coin to. The tract gives a brief past of his life and the sad steps that brought him to his fate. He frames it as the best last work he can do for the faith he hurt and for his land. His young faith and strong guilt open the tale.
72125-nibbles-poppelty-poppett:
Edith Davidson wrote Nibbles Poppelty-Poppett, the story of a mouse, printed at Boston in 1911. Pictures are by Clara Atwood. Davidson was known for the Bunnikins-Bunnies books. She gives the tale to her dormouse, from her friend the writer. Nibbles was a nice, plump little mouse, with bright black eyes and a silky grey coat.

He lived down a green lane near the river with his mother and his brothers and sisters. Sniffy and Snuffy, the twins, were always having colds together. Gobble was greedy, and Little Topsy was the baby. Their father came to a sad end, as the tale soon tells. Little children get a tender mouse family story, prettily pictured.
72232-an-index-to-the-collected-works-of:
Waller and Arnold Glover edited this index to the collected works of William Hazlitt, printed in London in 1906. Hazlitt, the great Romantic essayist, had his writings gathered in a many-volume set, and this book is the key that unlocks it. The editors dedicated the index to the memory of a helper whose initials close the volume.

A note explains the method: the index is confined, in the main, to the names of persons and things. Imaginary persons stand under the first word of their best-known name, so Tony Lumpkin is found under Tony. A heavy list of quotations follows, though phrases from Shakespeare and Milton were largely left out to save space. Scholars still use such tools daily.
73891-the-letters-of-robert-browning-and:
Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett wrote these love letters to each other in 1845 and 1846. This is the second of two volumes, in a second impression published in London in 1899. Portraits and facsimiles of the letters go with the text.

Browning first wrote to Barrett as a fan of her poems, and the exchange grew into one of the great courtships in literature. She was an invalid living under a stern father; he coaxed her back to life and, at last, to marriage in secret. The letters show wit, shyness, and rising boldness on both sides. Readers get two major poets falling in love in their own words.
75461-the-case-of-miss-elliott:
Baroness Orczy's The Case of Miss Elliott was published by Greening in London in 1909. Twelve cases fill the contents, all worked by the man in the corner: the hocussing of Cigarette, the tragedy in Dartmoor Terrace, the stolen black diamonds, and the murder of Miss Pebmarsh. The Lisson Grove mystery, the fate of the Artemis, and the affair at the Novelty Theatre stand among them.

The title case opens the book. The narrator watches the old man tie and untie his knots of string, and thinks of the mystery setting Scotland Yard by the ears. The Daily Telegraph had printed two columns headed Murder or Suicide, on the death of Miss Elliott, matron of the Convalescent Home in Suffolk Avenue. A frontispiece shows a hansom cab at night, its passenger dead in the shadowed interior, a man reaching in beside it.
75738-rebecca-jarrett:
Josephine Butler wrote this pamphlet on Rebecca Jarrett for Morgan and Scott of London, and it reached its tenth thousand. A cheap edition for distribution was priced at a penny, so the defence could travel widely.

Butler writes after the trial is over and tongues are loosed. She will not clear Jarrett of blame for wavering and for one plain falsehood under cross-examination about her past life. Instead she gives the woman's history, to show a situation that was pathetic, even tragic, with no human escape. Jarrett had acted for William Stead, Butler's friend, and Butler argues the press made her the scapegoat for every other prisoner's errors. The pamphlet pleads judgment, mercy, and faith for a fallen woman.
76027-the-poems-of-mary-howitt:
Mary Howitt was one of the best-loved English poets of her century, writing for children and for the fireside. This American edition of her poems came out in Philadelphia in 1844, with a memoir of her life. A portrait shows her in childhood.

The contents mix story poems such as The Poor Scholar with hymns and fireside verses. A long tale, Marien's Pilgrimage, runs in twelve parts. Other pieces mark Christmas, Easter, and the sorrows of the poor. Howitt and her husband William translated and wrote hundreds of books. Her plain, kind verse made her a household name on both sides of the Atlantic.
77345-the-rebellion-of-constable-kitt:
The Rebellion of Constable Kitt is a tale of the Mounted Police. Morris Longstreth wrote it, known as the force's own past teller. The voice is that of a man of the ranks in the stables. He hears the boys grouse at their chief and sets them straight.

The chief is a hard old hand, known by a cold nick name. He came from no one knew where in the days of the horse. He could ride any beast with hair, by his own first claim. The teller owns he backs the old man in the main grumps. His own beef is with the chief's views on horses as a class. He wants his horse power in a tin, with a clutch to let in. The clash of horse days and car days drives the tale.
77662-shades-of-davy-crockett:
Theodore Pratt wrote a fantasy of Davy Crockett loose in a modern city. A front note says Crockett fever had swept the nation for near two years. The big man walks the pavement in buckskin, coonskin cap, and long rifle. Moccasins pain his feet on the hard city streets, the tale notes.

A police officer asks if he holds a license to walk so armed. The man drawls his name as David Crockett and can not grasp the fuss. The officer warns him off the beat, sure a press stunt is afoot. Readers gain a warm fable of a hero at odds with a changed world.
77922-miss-lulu-bett:
Zona Gale wrote Miss Lulu Bett, first a novel and then this play, printed by Appleton in New York in 1921. The play won the Pulitzer prize of a thousand dollars in June 1921, for the American play that best raised the standard of morals, taste, and manners on the stage.

Gale calls it an American comedy of manners. Lulu Bett is the drudge sister in a small-town family, taken for granted by all. The play squeezes big feeling into a narrow kitchen world. A letter from Thomas Dickinson praises Gale's art of condensation: discourse refined to shorthand. The printed play keeps the prize citation at its front. It remains a landmark of American drama between the wars.
78565-a-mirror-of-shalott:
Robert Hugh Benson's A Mirror of Shalott, a set of tales told at an unprofessional symposium, was published by Benziger Brothers in 1907. Benson, a priest who had written The Sentimentalists, frames the book in talk. Thirteen tales follow a prologue, each named for its teller.

The tellers are mostly priests, gathered in the upstairs room of a presbytery in Rome, round a fire under dingy painted gods and nymphs. Monsignor Maxwell opens the prologue with an attack on common agnosticism: the man who says such things do not happen, he holds, is the most dogmatic of sectarians. Father Meuron, Father Brent, the Father Rector, and Father Girdlestone with three tales take the floor in turn.
78731-with-scott:
With Scott: The Silver Lining, by Griffith Taylor, is a geologist's tale of the Antarctic expedition. Smith, Elder printed the book in London in 1916. Nearly two hundred illustrations and maps fill it, many of them photographs.

A frontispiece shows the sledge-mates at Cambridge in November 1913, Taylor among them. The chapters get to know the men, then sail south in the Terra Nova. Geologists visit the New Zealand glaciers, and ship life runs from calm to storm. Pack ice blocks the way before the Ross Sea opens, and winter quarters rise at Cape Evans. A first western expedition and a month in the old Discovery hut follow. Winter quarters with Captain Scott fill the long middle. Granite Harbour, the voyage back, and the end of the expedition close the book.
8680-the-story-of-kennett:
Bayard Taylor sets this novel in Kennett, the Pennsylvania countryside he knew well, and dedicates it to his friends and neighbours there. In his prologue he tells them plainly that many will live in the very houses and till the very fields he gives his characters. Will judge whether he drew them with the simple truth he aimed at. He asks their pardon for any failure, and thanks them for quiet, happy years among them.

The story that follows grows out of that soil: farm families, local customs, love, and rivalry in a Quaker-influenced community. Taylor writes with a neighbour's eye for work, worship, and talk, rather than a tourist's romance. Readers of American regional fiction will find a warm, grounded novel. A portrait of Chester County life that its first readers could check against their own front doors.
9597-the-inner-life-part-3-from-the-work:
Part three of Whittier's Inner Life gathers essays on evil, faith, and the Quaker way. The Agency of Evil opens, asking where sin and suffering come from in a world full of mystery. Hamlet Among the Graves, Swedenborg, and The Better Land follow, with Dora Greenwell and The Society of Friends. John Woolman's Journal and Haverford College close the run.

Whittier weighs dark riddles with a Quaker's trust in inward light, not with cold systems. His prose stays plain and earnest, aimed at the heart. A reader gets a thoughtful set of spiritual essays, where a poet faces evil, death, and hope with quiet faith.
a-dream-of-empire-or-the-house-of-blenne: William Henry Venable tells a dream of empire through the house of Blennerhassett. An eccentric visitor arrives in Pittsburg, and pillars of smoke mark the chapters that follow. Conspiracy, a noted character, and a ladies bower shape the plot. Venable writes a historical romance of ambition on the American frontier.
a-master-of-fortune-being-further-advent: Cutcliffe Hyne sends Captain Kettle on further adventures as a master of fortune. Chapters open in quarantine, meet a little wooden god with eyes, and take a quick way with rebels. A new republic and the looting of the Indian Sheriff follow. Hyne writes sea adventure with Kettle's bold humor.
britannica-1911-a-beckett-gilbert-abbott:
Gilbert Abbott a Beckett, an English writer who lived from 1811 to 1856, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in north London in January 1811. His kin claimed descent from the father of St Thomas Becket, and his elder brother became chief justice of Victoria. Gilbert was schooled at Westminster and called to the bar in 1841.

He edited Figaro in London and was on the first staff of Punch, to which he wrote all his life. He worked as a journalist on The Times and The Morning Herald. He found time to write some fifty or sixty plays, among them stage forms of the short tales of Dickens. As a poor-law commissioner he wrote a valued report on the Andover Union scandal. In 1849 he became a police magistrate in London, and he died of fever at Boulogne in 1856.
britannica-1911-abbott-edwin-abbott:
Edwin Abbott Abbott receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbott, an English schoolmaster and theologian born in 1838, took top honours at Cambridge in classics, mathematics, and theology at once. City of London School made him headmaster in 1865, at twenty-six.

Retirement in 1889 freed him for books. His Shakespearian Grammar stands as a lasting gift to English philology, and a life of Francis Bacon followed. Three religious romances came out unnamed: Philochristus, Onesimus, and Silanus. The Kernel and the Husk and a bold Gospels article stirred the theological world. Johannine Vocabulary and Grammar closed his scholarly list. His brother Evelyn, the Balliol tutor and Greek historian, shares the final line of the entry.
britannica-1911-browning-elizabeth-barre:
Elizabeth Barrett Browning is the subject of this long biographical entry, though the hosted file opens mid-article, in the midst of her working years rather than at her birth. The portion present finds her writing two series of articles on the Greek Christian poets and on the English poets for the Athenaeum under C. W. Dilke. Drawing strength from work after heavy grief.

Her own quoted words carry the passage: once she wished not to live, yet the faculty of life sprang up again under grief's crushing foot. By 1842 Robert Browning's name enters her letters, noted as learned in Greek and not behind in praising her poet studies. The same year shows her declared love for Tennyson's verse. A letter from Wordsworth and his wish to visit, barred by her ill health, Haydon's unfinished portrait of Wordsworth on Helvellyn and her sonnet on it.
britannica-1911-burdon-sanderson-sir-joh:
Burdon-Sanderson, Sir John Scott, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English physiologist. Born at West Jesmond on the 21st of December 1828, he came of a Northumbrian house. He took his medical training at Edinburgh and at Paris. He then settled in London to practise his art.

In 1856 he became health officer for Paddington in London town. Four years later he was physician to two London hospitals. When diphtheria broke out in 1858 he was sent to probe it. Like probes into cattle plague and cholera came in later years. In 1874 he took a chair at University College in London. In 1882 he moved to a new chair at Oxford.
britannica-1911-burnside-ambrose-everett:
Ambrose Everett Burnside, who lived from 1824 to 1881, was an American soldier in a 1911 Britannica life. He was born at Liberty in Indiana to Scots stock in a log cabin home. A chance favour won him a place at the military academy, and he finished in 1847. He left the army in 1853 and made firearms at Bristol for five years.

In 1856 he devised a breech loading rifle that bore his name in use. Rail work filled his days until the Civil War broke out in 1861. He led a Rhode Island regiment to guard the capital at the start. He then led a brigade at the first battle of Bull Run.
britannica-1911-cairnes-john-elliott:
John Elliott Cairnes, a British writer on wealth and state who lived from 1823 to 1875, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in Ireland in 1823 and first worked in his father's brew house. His bent was for study, so he went to Trinity College, Dublin. He took degrees there and was called to the Irish bar.

Law held little charm for Cairnes, so he wrote for the press on Irish social and wealth themes. In 1856 he gained a chair in his field at Dublin. His first talks were printed in 1857 as a book on the method of the science. The piece praises its exact thought and clear tongue. His later book The Slave Power is also named.
britannica-1911-cameron-verney-lovett:
Verney Lovett Cameron, an English traveler in central Africa who lived from 1844 to 1894, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born near Weymouth on July 1, 1844. He joined the navy in 1857 and served in the Abyssinian war of 1868. He also worked to stop the East African slave trade.

In 1873 Cameron led a party sent to aid Livingstone. He met the men bearing Livingstone's body, yet pressed on to Lake Tanganyika. There he found the lake's outlet, the Lukuga River. He moved west and in 1875 reached the far coast. He was the first European to cross the region from sea to sea.
britannica-1911-cannstatt:
Cannstatt, also spelled Kannstatt, is a town of Germany in Württemberg, set in a fertile valley on both banks of the Neckar, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a town entry. It lies a short way from Stuttgart and has been part of that city since 1904. Its people in 1905 numbered about twenty six thousand.

Cannstatt is a railway centre, with churches of both main faiths, two bridges over the Neckar, and fine streets, promenades and gardens in its modern quarter. Its work includes railway plant, automobiles and machinery, with spinning, weaving, chemical works and a brewery. Fruit and vines are grown widely round it. A large passing population is drawn by its mineral springs, known since Roman times and valued for diseases of the throat and for weakness of the nerves. Near by stand the palaces of Rosenstein and Wilhelma, the latter built in the Moorish style.
britannica-1911-chantrey-sir-francis-leg:
Sir Francis Legatt Chantrey, an English carver in stone born in seventeen eighty two, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Norton near Sheffield, he was the son of a joiner who tilled a small farm. His father died when the boy was eight years old. His mother wed once more, and his trade was left to the choice of his friends.

At age sixteen he was on the point of a place with a food shop in Sheffield. Then he saw wood carve work in a shop pane and asked to be made a carver in its stead. He was set with a wood carver of that town. There he met a fine hand at the chalk line, who gave him hours in paint craft.
britannica-1911-consett:
Consett, a town district in the north west of Durham in England, is covered in a brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies south east of Newcastle on a branch rail line. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was nine thousand six hundred and ninety four. It is the hub of a thick tract of works and mines.

At Shotley Bridge near the town, a small spa draws note. A crew of German metal men set up shop there in the sixteen hundreds. They made swords and knives of high fame. That trade is gone now, and paper mills stand in its stead. Vast coal pits and iron works fill the district in the text. The note is short, but it ties spa, blade craft, paper, coal, and iron into a clear town sketch for the north east.
britannica-1911-fessenden-william-pitt:
William Pitt Fessenden is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Fessenden was an American statesman and money manager who lived from 1806 to 1869. He was born in New Hampshire and graduated at Bowdoin College in 1823. He studied law and settled in Portland, Maine. He served in the state legislature and then in the national House as a Whig.

The article tells how he won fame as a speaker against the spread of slavery. In 1854 he was chosen for the United States Senate. Within a fortnight he spoke against a bill on Kansas and Nebraska and became a force in the fight. He helped form the Republican party and was re-elected in 1859. As head of the Senate finance group, his work ranked next to the president's in funding the Union war. In 1864 he became secretary of the treasury.
britannica-1911-gellert-christian-furcht:
Christian Fürchtegott Gellert, German poet who lived from 1715 to 1769, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Hainichen in the Saxon Erzgebirge on 4 July 1715. After the famed school of St Afra in Meissen, he entered Leipzig University in 1734 to study church learning. He worked as a private tutor for two years after his degree.

Back at Leipzig from 1741 he wrote for a journal founded by men who had broken with an old master. Shyness and weak health killed his plan to enter the ministry. In 1745 he began to teach at the university on poetry, rhetoric, and style, with great success. He became a professor in 1751 and held the post till his death in 1769. Students and all classes held him in vast esteem.
britannica-1911-gibbs-oliver-wolcott:
Oliver Wolcott Gibbs (1822–1908) was an American chemist born at New York on the 21st of February 1822. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that he dropped the name Oliver early and trained first in medicine, qualifying in 1845. He then studied in Germany and Paris under masters such as Liebig and Dumas.

In 1848 he became professor of chemistry at the Free Academy in New York. In 1863 he took the Rumford professorship at Harvard, which he held until he retired in 1887. His research lay chiefly in weighing and testing substances and in inorganic chemistry, above all the cobalt compounds, the platinum metals, and complex acids. He was held an excellent teacher and wrote many papers for the learned journals.
britannica-1911-hill-david-bennett:
David Bennett Hill (1843–1910) was an American politician, born at Havana, New York, in 1843. Admitted to the bar at Elmira in 1864, he rose fast in the Democratic party as a lieutenant of Samuel J. Tilden. He sat in the State Assembly in 1871–1872 and chaired the state convention twice.

In 1882 Hill became mayor of Elmira and lieutenant-governor of New York, after losing the governor nomination to Grover Cleveland. When Cleveland resigned for the presidency in January 1885, Hill succeeded him as governor. He sat in the United States Senate from 1891 to 1897, working against Cleveland. After 1897 he returned to law, and he died at Albany in 1910.
britannica-1911-millais-sir-john-everett:
Sir John Everett Millais, an English painter born in eighteen twenty nine, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Southampton, he was the son of a man of an old Norman house long set in Jersey. The family went back to Jersey soon past his birth. There the boy took to sketch at a young age.

At age eight he drew his grand sire on his mother side. He went to school for a short span but showed no bent for study. His mother taught him at home from that time. The family moved to a town in Brittany for two years. There the boy sketched French officers, to their great mirth. Back in Jersey a hired man taught him to draw. In eighteen thirty eight he came to London. A great man of art gave a strong word for his gift, and his path was set.
britannica-1911-ridge-william-pett:
William Pett Ridge, an English author born in eighteen sixty four, came from Chartham near Canterbury. He was schooled at Marden in Kent and at the Birkbeck Institute in London. For some time he worked as a clerk in the Railway Clearing House. About eighteen ninety one he began to write comic sketches for papers. The Saint James's Gazette was among the papers that took his work.

His first strong success in book form came with a novel in eighteen ninety eight. That book showed his gift for comic portraits of lower class life. Later books followed in quick order over the next eight years. Their titles include A Son of the State and Lost Property. Erb and Mrs Caler's Business are also named in the entry's list. His work kept the same comic touch and low life setting.
britannica-1911-russell-john-scott:
John Scott Russell, a British engineer who lived from 1808 to 1882, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Glasgow, he was a son of the manse and was first meant for the ministry. That plan changed when the boy showed an early bent for practical science. He went to the universities of Saint Andrews, Edinburgh, and Glasgow in turn, and took his degree at Glasgow at age sixteen.

After two years in workshops Russell settled in Edinburgh as a lecturer on science and drew large classes. In 1832 he was called to give the natural philosophy course at the university in a vacant chair. The next year he began his famed long series of tests on waves. A question about steam boats on the Edinburgh and Glasgow canal set that work in train.
britannica-1911-scrope-george-julius-pou:
George Julius Poulett Scrope, who lived from 1797 to 1876, was an English geologist and writer on public finance. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the tenth of March 1797. He was schooled at Harrow and went to Cambridge, where talks with Clarke and Sedgwick turned him to rocks. A winter at Naples in 1816 fired his zeal for Vesuvius. He went back in 1818 and then toured Etna and the Lipari Islands.

In 1821 Scrope wed the heiress of Castle Combe and took her name. He sat in parliament for Stroud from 1833 to 1868. His book on volcanoes of 1825 set out a new view of the earth. A great memoir on the dead volcanoes of central France came in 1827. The Geological Society gave him its Wollaston Medal in 1867.
britannica-1911-sestett:
Sestett names the second part of a sonnet, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A sonnet must have an octave of eight lines first. Six lines follow to make the sestett. The rhymes often run in a set pattern of two groups of three. That pattern is not a strict rule.

Early Italian sonnets, and those of Dante most of all, often close with a crossed rhyme scheme. In tongues with less rich sound than Italian, a gap of five lines between rhymes is risky. The quatorzain has no true sestett, but a quatrain and a couplet, as in the sonnets of Shakespeare. A sestett should mark the turn of feeling in the poem. Thought and personal voice tend to enter there, after the more outward octave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eichstatt:
Eichstatt is a diocese in Bavaria, north of the Danube and suffragan to Bamberg, whose story the entry traces from its founding to 1909. Saint Boniface set it up, making his nephew Saint Willibald abbot and regional bishop in 741 and fixing the diocese in 745. Willibald brought his brother Wunibald and sister Walburga to help, built Heidenheim monastery for them, and ran a flourishing school at Eichstatt until his death in 781.

His successors number seventy-five in an unbroken line. Bishop Erchanbold laid the ground for the see's worldly power. It grew through the Hirschberg inheritance of 1305. By then the bishops ruled a land of some four hundred and thirty-seven square miles and fifty-six thousand people. Secularisation in 1803 handed those lands to Bavaria. Among the bishops, Reginold shone as poet and musician, and Gundekar II rebuilt the cathedral and wrote its bishops' lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-xavie:
Francis Xavier Witt, born at Walderbach in the Upper Palatinate on 9 February 1834 and dead at Landshut on 2 December 1888. He was a priest, composer, and reformer of church music who founded the St. Cecilia Society for German-speaking lands. Ordained on 11 June 1856, he served as assistant pastor while studying music in all its branches.

In 1859 he became teacher of Gregorian chant, homiletics, and catechetics at the Ratisbon seminary, then director of the Sodality of the Blessed Virgin and choirmaster at St. Emmeran. His compositions, more than twenty masses for voices with organ, orchestra, or unaccompanied, plus litanies, motets, and music for the whole liturgical year, remain standard repertoire in the best choirs. They are praised for fine construction, spontaneity, and organic cohesion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspar-schott:
Gaspar Schott, a German Jesuit physicist born at Königshofen in 1608, woke scientific curiosity across Germany. He entered the Society in 1627, finished his studies in Sicily amid political turmoil, taught at Palermo, and studied under Kircher at Rome. After some thirty years abroad he returned home and spent his last years teaching and writing at Augsburg, dying in 1666.

Schott's books overflow with curious facts and trials, once widely read. His Universal Magic of Nature and Art, four volumes from 1657 to 1659, gathers mathematical puzzles and trials in optics and sound. His Hydraulic-Pneumatic Mechanics gave the first printed account of Guericke's air pump. A Curious Physics, a study of springs and rivers, and a mathematics course followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-robert-:
Parliamentary barrister James Robert Hope-Scott, originally Hope, was born at Great Marlow, Berkshire, on 15 July 1812. He died in London on 29 April 1873. He was third son of Sir Alexander Hope, fourth son of John, second Earl of Hopetoun. His mother was the third and youngest daughter of George Brown of Ellerton. During childhood his home was Sandhurst Military College, where his father commanded. Afterwards he traveled with his parents through Dresden, Lausanne, and Florence.

Thus he mastered German, French, and Italian. In 1825 he entered Eton, and in 1828 he matriculated at Christ Church, Oxford. After a Paris visit in 1829 he took up Oxford residence that year. He took his B.A. in 1832, placing fourth class in literis humanioribus. Next year he became a fellow of Merton College. The entry opens the life of a Tractarian lawyer whose scholarship and conversions shaped Victorian Catholicism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-hewett:
John Hewett, also recorded as Weldon, was an English martyr executed in the Armada year of 1588. Son of William Hewett of York, he passed from Caius College, Cambridge, to the English College at Reims, where he received minor orders in 1583. Captured in England and banished, he reached Reims again in 1585, was ordained, and returned, only to be captured and exiled to the Netherlands.

There the Earl of Leicester had him arrested on a false accusation and sent back for trial. In October 1588 he was arraigned for taking ordination from Rome and entering England to work as a priest. Sentenced to death, he was taken through London streets to Mile End Green, where before execution he disputed with two preachers. That the two names denote one martyr is proved by a tract of 24 October 1588 reporting the trial and speeches of Weldon, Hartley, and Sutton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joshua-basset:
Joshua Bassett was an English scholar who became Master of Sidney Sussex College under James II. Born about 1641 at Lynn Regis, he entered Gonville and Caius College in 1657, took degrees through 1671, and rose to senior fellow. By the king's mandate he was elected Master of Sidney Sussex in December 1686 without the usual oaths.

In January 1687 Bassett declared himself a Catholic, had Mass said in his rooms, and changed statutes that barred his co-religionists. He clashed with the university over a degree for the Benedictine Alban Francis and banned a Guy Fawkes Day service. After the Revolution he fled the college and died in extreme poverty at London in 1720.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquard-herr:
Marquard Herrgott was a Benedictine historian and diplomat, born at Freiburg in 1694 and dead at Krozingen in 1762. After humanities at Freiburg and Strasburg, he tutored a private family and followed two pupils to Paris for two years. On return he joined St Blasien Abbey in the Black Forest, vowing in 1715 and studying theology at Rome.

Ordained in 1718, he returned to St Blasien, studied Oriental tongues at St Gall in 1721, and soon went to Vienna with his abbot to study history. He then worked under Maurist Benedictines at Saint-Germain-des-Pres, producing Vetus disciplina monastica at Paris in 1726 on old monastic customs. In 1728 Vienna made him diplomatic envoy of the Breisgau Estates, a post he held creditably over twenty years. There he studied Habsburg history for eight years and published his Genealogia diplomatica in 1737, followed by Monumenta volumes in 1750, 1753, and 1760.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missal-of-arb:
The Missal of Arbuthnott is a handwritten Scottish Mass book, penned in 1491 by James Sibbald, priest of Arbuthnott in Scotland, for his own church. After the Reformation it came, along with two further manuscripts in the same hand, into the Arbuthnott family's keeping, where it stayed until 1897.

In that year Archibald Coats of Paisley bought it and presented it to the Paisley museum. The manuscript, written on vellum in large Gothic characters with numerous miniatures, illuminated capitals, and borders, consists of 244 leaves and is complete. It also contains a full-length painting of St. Ternan, the patron of Arbuthnott, making it a treasure of late medieval Scottish devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-hardema:
Peter Hardeman Burnett was the first American governor of California, born at Nashville in 1807. Raised in Missouri's rough conditions, he married Harriet Rogers, studied law, was admitted to the bar in 1839, and edited a Missouri weekly. Moving to Oregon in 1843, he helped frame its territorial government and sat in its legislature. A published debate between Alexander Campbell and Bishop Purcell shook his Protestant faith.

Systematic study led him to Rome, and he was received into the Catholic Church at Oregon City in June 1846. In California from 1848 he sat in the assembly, became a superior court judge in 1849, helped frame the state constitution, and served as chief justice. That November he was chosen governor, the first to hold the office under American statehood. He died at San Francisco in 1895.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-wes:
Sebastian Westcott, English organist born about 1524, sang as a boy chorister at St Paul's Cathedral in London under Redford. In 1550 he took three posts there at once: organist, almoner, and master of the boys. He held his post under Edward VI, Mary, and Elizabeth from 1550 to 1583, despite standing openly for the ancient faith, for which he suffered deprivation and prison. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia celebrates Master Sebastian.

His fame rests chiefly on plays and pageants with music, staged for the English court over thirty-three years by the cathedral schoolboys. So celebrated was he that writers seldom use his surname, calling him almost always Master Sebastian. Under Mary he arranged music for the formal restoration of the old faith at St Paul's in November 1553. He also composed a Te Deum sung on 9 February 1554 after Wyatt's rebellion failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-edward:
Thomas Edward Bridgett, priest and author, was born at Derby in 1829 to Protestant parents and died at Clapham in 1899. His father, a silk manufacturer, sent him to Mill Hill, Tonbridge and St. John's College, Cambridge. Unable to swear the oath of royal supremacy, he left Cambridge in 1850, heard Newman lecture, and was received into the Catholic Church that June.

He joined the Redemptorists in Belgium and was ordained in 1856. He served at Clapham and Limerick, where in 1868 he founded the Confraternity of the Holy Family for men, soon over five thousand strong. As a writer he is best known for lives of John Fisher and other English Catholic figures, blending scholarship with missionary zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-james-duc:
James Duckett was a martyr born at Gilfortrigs in Skelsmergh parish, Westmoreland, at an uncertain date, of an ancient county family, who died on 9 April 1601. He worked as a bookseller and publisher in London. His godfather was the martyr James Leybourn of Skelsmergh. Brought up Protestant, he was converted while an apprentice in London by a Catholic book a friend lent him.

Before he could enter the church he was twice jailed for skipping Protestant service, and he had to buy out his apprenticeship and leave his master. At last a venerable priest named Weekes, jailed in the Gatehouse at Westminster, reconciled him. After two or three years he married a Catholic widow. Of twelve years of married life no fewer than nine were spent in prison, for spreading Catholic books and holding fast to his new-found faith, before his arrest and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-duck:
John Duckett was a martyr, probably a grandson of James Duckett, born at Underwinder in Sedbergh parish, Yorkshire, in 1603, who died on 7 September 1644. Ordained priest in 1639, he then went to Paris and studied three years at the College of Arras. He possessed an extraordinary gift of prayer, and even as a student he would spend whole nights in contemplation.

En route to the English mission, he passed two months in spiritual exercises guided by his uncle, Nieuport's Carthusian prior. He laboured about a year in Durham and was seized near Whittingham on his way to baptize two children on 2 July 1644. Tradition marks his arrest place with a tall stone cross. Carried to Sunderland, examined by a Parliamentary committee, and put in irons, he was condemned and suffered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-montford-:
Montford Scott was an English martyr born in Norfolk, martyred at Fleet Street in London on 2 July 1591. He entered Douai College in 1574, among its earliest students, and studied theology. The next year he became subdeacon and accompanied Dominic Vaughan to England. In Essex they fell into government hands in December 1576, and under examination Vaughan weakly betrayed the names of Catholics in London and Essex.

Handed by the Privy Council to the Archbishop of Canterbury for further questioning, they gave up nothing more and were afterwards set free. Scott returned to Douai on 22 May 1577, was ordained priest at Brussels, and set out for the English mission on 17 June. His crossing vessel was attacked by pirates, but he escaped with his life. The entry follows his later mission years and his execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-ralph-cro:
Ralph Crockett was an English martyr born at Barton near Farndon in Cheshire, executed at Chichester on 1 October 1588. Schooled at Cambridge and ordained at Reims in 1585, he was captured aboard ship at Littlehampton in Sussex with three other priests. They were Thomas Bramston, George Potter, and his fellow martyr Edward James, born at Breaston in Derbyshire about 1557.

James was schooled at Derby Grammar School, then St John's College, Oxford, and the English colleges at Reims and Rome, before Bishop Goldwell of St Asaph ordained him in October 1583. All four were sent to London and jailed on 27 April 1586. After the Armada's failure the government resolved to avenge itself on priests in custody. Crockett and James, with John Oven and Francis Edwardes, were chosen for trial at Chichester on 30 September and executed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-tho:
Thomas Sprott, or Spratt, was a Westmorland priest executed at Lincoln in July 1600 with Thomas Hunt. Born at Skelsmergh near Kendal, Sprott was ordained from Douai in 1596, sent to England the same year. Signed a 1598 letter to the pope favouring an archpriest, a chief priest, for England.

Hunt, a Norfolk priest trained at Seville, had escaped from Wisbech prison months earlier. The two were arrested at the Saracen's Head in Lincoln when holy oils and two breviaries, priests' prayer books, were found in their baggage. At trial neither priesthood was proved nor confessed and no evidence was produced, yet Judge Sir John Glanville directed the jury to convict, which it did. Glanville died sixteen days later under unusual circumstances, as the entry records.
cicero-catilinarian-orations-upcott:
Cicero's Catilinarian Orations are four speeches he gave in 63 BC as consul of Rome, against the conspirator Catiline. E. A. Upcott's Oxford translation is the text here. Catiline, a ruined aristocrat, was plotting to seize the state with an army raised in Etruria.

The first speech, delivered in the Senate with Catiline present, opens with the famous cry: how long will you abuse our patience? Cicero lays out the plot, drives Catiline from the city, and reports the arrest of his partners in Rome. The speeches saved the republic and made Cicero's name as an orator. They have been school models of rhetoric ever since.
doe-osti-3012257-evaluating-movement-pat:
Movement patterns of the Rattlesnake Hills elk herd on the Hanford Site are evaluated by J. J. Nugent and C. T. Lindsey in HNF-71433, covering calendar years 2019 to 2024. Aerial surveys, ground driving surveys, and incidental observations feed the analysis. Eleven ground surveys ran between January 2021 and January 2024.

Central Hanford counts reached 396 elk in winter and fell as low as 27 in summer. Aerial surveys in the same weeks detected more animals, so ground counts understate the herd. Incidental observations from December 2019 to August 2024 recorded 375 unique locations, from single animals to herds of 600. The data support core use modelling for the herd.
doe-osti-3024733-new-correlated-numerica:
Luca Argenti reports his Early Career award DE-SC0020311, which produced ASTRA, a code for molecular ionization on attosecond timescales. Attosecond pulses of extreme ultraviolet and soft x-ray light can now start and watch electrons leaving a molecule. Modeling that process with electrons properly correlated, in single and double ionization, is the hard part ASTRA was built for.

Pieces of the platform include the PRISM hybrid-integral library, which helps core ionization and high angular momentum cases settle, and time-dependent Schrödinger equation solvers for pump-probe setups. The code was checked against experimental and theory benchmarks for atoms and molecules, then extended to two-photon double ionization. A list of papers runs from a 2021 multi-center integration paper to molecular-frame photoelectron studies of carbon monoxide near Feshbach resonances.
doe-osti-3409467-theoretical-high-energy:
Luchang Jin of the University of Connecticut reports on lattice methods in high energy physics under award DE-SC0026314. The project period ran from July 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026. Much of the work was done with the RBC and UKQCD collaborations.

One study computed QED corrections to meson decay, testing whether electrons and muons behave alike. That ratio gives a clean check of lepton flavor universality. Other work covered form factors for pion and kaon decays, with results at two lattice spacings. Physicists gain sharper theory numbers to set against precise experiment data.
doe-osti-3683731-mach-14-thermometry-usi:
Sandia report SAND2025-12421R covers early tests of a laser method for gas temperature in a Mach 14 wind tunnel. Will Senior and Daniel Richardson are the two named team members. At Mach 14, tunnel gas sits near thirty kelvin and very low pressure. Raman scattering, which works at Mach 8 and below, loses its feel for temperature there. The team turned to coherent Rayleigh scattering, which reads the spread of molecular speeds instead.

Old Rayleigh setups needed over ten minutes of scanning for one reading, far past a forty-five-second tunnel run. The new setup uses a highly dispersive optic and a picosecond laser to take a reading in one pulse. Bench tests first proved the single-shot method in room air. A cold vacuum chamber then mimicked tunnel conditions. Signal stayed strong enough to fit temperature at densities tied to Mach 14 flow.
general-scott:
Marcus J. Wright, himself a general, wrote this life of Winfield Scott for the Great Commanders series, edited by James Grant Wilson and published in 1894. Scott served the United States Army longer than almost any other officer. Wright follows him from youth through the War of 1812, the war with Mexico, and the first months of the Civil War.

Scott's fame rests on his march to Mexico City and on his skill at drill and supply. Wright also shows the man's pride, his feuds, and his care for his troops. Portraits and a series frame link Scott to peers such as Farragut, Taylor, and Jackson. The book is a respectful, fact-filled life by a fellow soldier, written while many who served under Scott still lived.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BremerGeorgeWal:
Arthur Bremer shot George Wallace in May 1972, crippling the Alabama governor during his presidential campaign. This Washington Post article by Philip A. McCombs reports what Bremer's diary revealed: before Wallace, his intended target had been President Richard Nixon.

The diary describes Bremer following Nixon back to Washington from Ottawa in April 1972, after missing six chances to shoot him there. Bremer wrote his way toward an assassination, and the diary became the record of that drift. The article preserves the news as it broke, when the Wallace shooting suddenly looked like the second act of a plan aimed at a president.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JacksonEverett_:
Fenton Wheeler reported for the Associated Press under the headline Plane Blasted. Cuba had shot down and captured Everett Jackson, an American former paratrooper. Jackson's flight ended after he dropped a package containing a rifle over Cuba on December 29.
